title: Is Tooth Extraction Painful? Pain, Recovery and What to Eat
seoTitle: Is Tooth Extraction Painful? Recovery and Aftercare
description: How much a tooth extraction typically hurts, how long it lasts, what to eat each day, and the warning signs to call about, from Dr. Moezzi in Valencia.
excerpt: Extraction pain typically peaks within 48 hours and eases from there. Here is what to expect, what to eat each day, and when to call the office.
author: Dr. Neda Moezzi, DDS
imageAlt: A soft-food meal on a wooden table: a bowl of lukewarm soup with a spoon, mashed avocado, scrambled eggs and a glass of water
keyTakeaways: Extractions are done under local anesthesia, and post-operative pain typically peaks in the first 24 to 48 hours before easing.
Simple extractions often settle in 3 to 7 days; surgical or impacted wisdom tooth removals can take two weeks or longer.
Protecting the blood clot, with no straws, no smoking and a soft-food progression, is the main way to avoid dry socket.

body:
If you have an extraction scheduled, or just left the chair, the first question is usually about pain. This guide explains how much discomfort to expect, how long it typically lasts, what to eat while the socket heals, and which warning signs mean you should call. For procedure details and your own written instructions, start with our [tooth extraction service page](/services/oral-surgery/tooth-extractions/). Dr. Neda Moezzi performs extractions in our Valencia office and reviews aftercare with you before you leave.

## Does a tooth extraction hurt?

Nearly all extractions are done under local anesthesia, so you feel pressure but little or no pain during the procedure itself. Sedation options are available when appropriate. Once the numbness fades, some soreness is normal. Guidance from the American Association of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgeons and the Mayo Clinic describes the same pattern: pain usually peaks in the first 24 to 48 hours and eases over the following days. A simple extraction often settles within 3 to 7 days. A surgical extraction or an impacted wisdom tooth can be more uncomfortable and may take two weeks or longer before you feel mostly normal.

## A typical pain timeline

Clinical experience and patient reports follow a predictable curve.

| Procedure type | Peak pain | Most people functional | Soft tissue comfortable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Simple extraction | 24 to 48 hours | 3 to 7 days | About 2 weeks |
| Surgical extraction or impacted wisdom tooth | 24 to 72 hours | 7 to 14 days | 3 to 4 weeks |

Pain that improves day by day is expected. Pain that gets worse after the third day is not, and it needs a clinical look rather than more pain medication.

## Why what you eat matters

Two things are happening in the socket at once. A blood clot forms and protects the bone underneath, and your body begins rebuilding tissue. If the clot is dislodged, the result can be dry socket, a painful condition that delays healing. At the same time, protein, vitamin C, zinc, calcium and fluids give your body what it needs to repair. The NHS and the American Dental Association both stress mechanical protection and nutrition as the two pillars of a smooth recovery.

## Five rules for the first week

- **No straws.** Suction can pull the clot loose. Skip straws for at least 7 to 10 days.
- **Spoon, do not sip.** Eat smoothies and soups with a spoon, or drink directly from a cup.
- **Soft and nutrient dense.** Favor spoonable foods with protein and vitamins.
- **Cool to lukewarm.** Very hot food and drink can increase bleeding and swelling.
- **Small bites on the other side.** When solids return, chew away from the extraction site.

## Eating plan by phase

Adjust for allergies and medical conditions, and follow any instructions specific to your case.

### Days 0 to 2: spoonable, cool to lukewarm

The goals are to protect the clot, limit bleeding and swelling, and keep up fluids and calories.

- Greek yogurt or plain yogurt (no seeds or granola)
- Protein smoothie eaten with a spoon (blend with Greek yogurt or protein powder)
- Clear broth or strained soup, lukewarm
- Applesauce, mashed banana, mashed avocado
- Soft scrambled eggs

### Days 3 to 7: thicker purees and soft solids

Add texture gradually while still protecting the socket.

- Oatmeal or cream of wheat, cooled to lukewarm
- Mashed potatoes or mashed sweet potato
- Flaked or poached white fish
- Soft tofu or mashed cooked legumes
- Soft pasta or risotto

### Weeks 1 to 2 and beyond: back to normal textures

Return to your regular diet as comfort and your clinician allow.

- Ground or shredded meat and tender cuts
- Soft fruit cut into small pieces
- Vegetables steamed until fork tender
- After a surgical extraction, avoid crunchy, sticky or very hard foods for about four weeks

## Foods to avoid in the first 2 to 8 weeks

| Category | Examples | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crunchy | Chips, nuts, popcorn | Particles can lodge in the socket and irritate it |
| Sticky | Caramel, chewing gum | Can pull on sutures or dislodge the clot |
| Very hot | Hot drinks or soup right after surgery | Can increase bleeding and swelling |
| Smoking and alcohol | Cigarettes, alcoholic drinks during early healing | Delay healing and raise infection risk |

## Sample 3-day meal plan

Easy to eat, with enough protein and vitamins to support repair.

| Day | Breakfast | Lunch | Snack or dinner |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Day 1 | Greek yogurt with mashed banana | Strained chicken broth, protein smoothie by spoon | Applesauce, soft scrambled egg |
| Day 3 | Oatmeal with mashed berries | Pureed vegetable soup with blended lentils | Poached flaked fish with mashed potato |
| Day 7 | Soft omelet with avocado | Soft pasta with pureed vegetable sauce and shredded chicken | Ground turkey meatball with mashed sweet potato |

## Pain control and medication

Most people manage post-operative pain with scheduled over-the-counter anti-inflammatories such as ibuprofen, with acetaminophen added when appropriate. Opioids are rarely needed and are reserved for more extensive surgical cases. Take medication as directed, and check with us before combining anything with your other prescriptions. If antibiotics were prescribed, finish the course unless told otherwise. If swelling returns after a course of antibiotics, that calls for a reassessment, not a second round on your own.

## Two questions patients ask often

First, patients in orthodontic treatment ask when they can put an Invisalign tray back in. Clinicians generally want the socket to show early healing and swelling to be under control before applying orthodontic force, often one to two weeks after a simple extraction. Tell both your surgeon and your orthodontist so they can coordinate. Second, patients ask whether recurring swelling is normal. It is not. Persistent or returning symptoms can point to retained debris, resistant bacteria or another problem, and they need to be seen.

## When to call the office

Call right away if you notice any of the following:

- Pain that increases after 72 hours instead of improving
- Heavy bleeding that soaks through gauze every 30 to 60 minutes
- Fever above 100.4°F (38°C) or swelling that worsens quickly
- A foul taste or drainage from the socket
- Difficulty breathing or swallowing

These can signal infection, dry socket or another complication that needs prompt care. The NHS guide to [dental abscess](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/dental-abscess/) explains why early contact matters.

## Related reading

For recovery after implant surgery, see [Do dental implants hurt? Recovery and pain](/do-dental-implants-hurt-recovery-pain-healing-guide/) and our nutrition guide, [Best foods after dental implant surgery](/best-foods-after-dental-implant-surgery/). If you are in orthodontic treatment, let us know so extraction timing and appliance schedules line up.

## The short answer

Expect short-term pain that typically peaks within the first 48 hours and improves with proper pain control and aftercare. Protect the clot, follow a soft-food progression for the first week, prioritize protein, and call if pain or swelling worsens. For personalized advice on diet, pain control or coordination with orthodontic care, [schedule a follow-up](/contact/) or call (661) 254-5200.

faq.q: How long after a tooth extraction can I eat solid food?
faq.a: Many patients can start soft solids after 3 to 7 days, depending on comfort and whether the extraction was simple. Begin with small, soft pieces and chew away from the surgical side. Your clinician will confirm when the socket is stable enough for firmer textures.

faq.q: How long after a tooth extraction should I wait to insert my Invisalign tray?
faq.a: Timing varies. Most clinicians want the socket to show early healing and swelling to be under control before orthodontic force is applied, often one to two weeks after a simple extraction. Ask both your surgeon and your orthodontist so they can coordinate.

faq.q: What foods help prevent dry socket?
faq.a: Soft, spoonable, protein-rich foods lower the risk of disturbing the clot: Greek yogurt, pureed soups, mashed potatoes, soft fish, and smoothies eaten with a spoon. Avoid crunchy, sticky or hard items that could dislodge it.

faq.q: My swelling returned after antibiotics. Should I worry?
faq.a: Yes. Swelling that returns after antibiotics needs a clinical reassessment. Persistent or worsening symptoms can point to retained debris, resistant bacteria or another issue. Call the office rather than extending antibiotics on your own.

faq.q: Can I use smoothies for all meals after extraction?
faq.a: Smoothies are convenient early on, but skip the straw. Eat them with a spoon and include protein such as Greek yogurt or protein powder. Limit added sugar and add vegetables or healthy fats for balance.

faq.q: When can I smoke or drink alcohol after extraction?
faq.a: Do not smoke for at least 72 hours, and preferably longer, because smoking delays healing and raises dry socket risk. Avoid alcohol while taking antibiotics or opioid pain medication and during early healing. Your surgeon will advise a timeline for your case.
